entries.name: Vietnamese Catholicism — Vicars Apostolic and Catechists
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1). Its window opens in 1650, but its roots lie in the 1620s, which no earlier entry carries. It is told in two parts, split at 1815, as the Philippine entries are.
entries.sourcing: Thin in Vietnamese voices. Almost every text is a missionary's: the histories of the Paris mission by Adrien Launay, the decrees of Propaganda, and a catechism by the Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes. The one Vietnamese voice is the priest Philiphê Bỉnh, whom George Dutton reads. His own book was not read for this entry.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed. The catechism of 1651 gives a date only; its title page was read, not its teaching.
entries.relationsSummary: This church began with the Jesuits of the Portuguese mission in the 1620s. From 1658 Rome sent its own bishops, called vicars apostolic, and the Paris mission supplied the priests. The Jesuits' old flock refused the new bishops. The same church goes on in the next entry, from 1815.
entries.why: Jesuits of the Portuguese mission began this church in the 1620s. In 1658 the pope made two French priests bishops, to act as Rome's own vicars in the missions of China and the lands nearby. Pallu was to lead Tonkin and Lambert de la Motte Cochinchina. Their coming set the Portuguese crown against the pope for more than a century. Rome's plan was to raise priests from Vietnam's own catechists.
entries.teaser: Vietnam, 1650 to 1815 — a church begun by Jesuits of the Portuguese mission and then ruled by bishops from Rome. Vietnamese catechists, priests and sisters carried it on.
entries.longDescription:
Jesuits sent under the Portuguese crown began the Catholic mission in Tonkin in the 1620s. Among them was the French Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes. The mission ran under the Padroado, the Portuguese king's patronage over the church in Asia. Some estimates put Tonkin's Christians at 80,000 in 1639 and 350,000 in 1663. The figures vary a great deal. In 1651 a catechism by Rhodes was printed at Rome, in Latin and Vietnamese, at the press of Propaganda, the Roman office for the missions.

In 1658 Propaganda proposed Pallu and Lambert de la Motte as vicars apostolic for China and its neighbors. In August the pope named them bishops. Dutton dates their choice as vicars to 1660. Pallu took Tonkin and Laos, and Lambert took Cochinchina. A vicar apostolic answered to the pope, not to the Portuguese crown. A new Paris mission society, the MEP, was set up to send them priests. The first vicars wrote a rule book for missionaries, the Monita. It said that native priests should be chosen from the catechists.

Lambert de la Motte reached Tonkin in 1670. He ordained seven priests. He gave lower orders to 48 Vietnamese converts. A month later he held the first synod in Vietnam. That year he also founded the Lovers of the Cross, a community of women. In 1673 Pope Clement X accepted the synod's decisions. In 1675 Rome granted indulgences to their groups in Tonkin and Cochinchina.

In 1678 Tonkin was split into an eastern and a western vicariate. The Paris mission kept the west. The east went to the Dominicans after 1693. The Jesuits' old flock, the Padroado Christians, kept their loyalty to Portugal. When the Jesuit order was dissolved in 1773, they refused to obey the vicars. They were called schismatics and kept from the sacraments. In 1796 the priest Philiphê Bỉnh sailed to Lisbon to ask the Portuguese ruler for a bishop for them.
voices: Alexandre de Rhodes — the Jesuit whose catechism in Latin and Vietnamese was printed at Rome in 1651
François Pallu and Pierre Lambert de la Motte — the two French priests Propaganda proposed as vicars apostolic in 1658
Philiphê Bỉnh — a catechist from the age of 17 and a priest at 34, who sailed to Lisbon in 1796 to ask for a bishop for his community
entries.legacy: The century ended with the church under three kinds of rule. The Paris mission held western Tonkin and the south. The Dominicans held eastern Tonkin. The Padroado Christians had no bishop of their own, and Bỉnh had gone to Lisbon to ask for one.

entries.name: Vietnamese Catholicism — Edicts and French Conquest
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Strong (Tier 1) for the church as a whole. Its verified base is thin after 1833. Its window opens in 1815, where the first part ends, and closes in 1906.
entries.sourcing: Thin. For 1815 to 1833 the main text is Adrien Launay's history of the Paris mission (1893), a priest's account of his own society. For the later years the entry rests on a short summary by the historian George Dutton. No Vietnamese Catholic's own words from these decades were read for this entry.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
entries.relationsSummary: It carries on the Vietnamese Catholic story from 1815. After Bỉnh died, probably in 1833, the story of the Padroado Christians joined the common story of Tonkin's Catholics. The emperor's edicts and then French conquest set the terms of church life.
entries.why: In 1832 the Paris mission, the MEP, counted between 160,000 and 170,000 Christians in Tonkin. Its bishop was Joseph Havard. It had about sixty native priests and thirty convents. A year later the emperor Minh Mạng issued his first great edict against them.
entries.teaser: Vietnam, 1815 to 1906 — a church with its own priests, catechists and sisters, under the emperor's edicts and then French conquest.
entries.longDescription:
Under the emperor Gia Long, Catholics were allowed to keep their religious practices. Most still bore labor and military service, like other Vietnamese. Minh Mạng came to power in 1820. He stressed orthodoxy in the state's teaching, and that left little room for practices at odds with Confucian rules. Dutton writes that his suspicion of Catholics and European missionaries led to periodic crackdowns and the public execution of priests. In Lisbon in 1822 Philiphê Bỉnh ended the story part of his book, written in Vietnamese. "I do not know how much longer I will live," he wrote, "but I ask that my brothers remember my soul." That is Dutton's English rendering. He probably died there in March 1833.

In 1832 the Paris mission, the MEP, counted 160,000 to 170,000 Christians in Tonkin. Its bishop was Joseph Havard. Launay lists about sixty native priests, several hundred catechists, and thirty convents with 400 sisters. They were the Lovers of the Cross, founded in 1670.

On 6 January 1833 Minh Mạng issued the first great edict against the Christians. It told them to give up their faith. It told the mandarins to make them trample the cross. It ordered their churches and the priests' houses razed.

Later in the century French pressure grew. Dutton writes that the French invasion brought large massacres of Catholics in the north-center. France then held the south and ruled the center and north as protectorates. Catholics gained protection. The taint of the French tie lingered.
voices: Philiphê Bỉnh — Vietnamese priest in Lisbon, who ended the story part of his book in Vietnamese there in 1822 and probably died there in March 1833
Minh Mạng — emperor from 1820, whose edict of 6 January 1833 ordered Christians to give up their faith
entries.legacy: In 1832 the church had about sixty native priests and thirty convents of the Lovers of the Cross, founded in 1670. Its tie to the French, formed in conquest, left a taint that lingered. Dutton notes that this began to change by the century's end.

entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window runs from 1650 to 1815. Its roots go back to 1605, when the Company took Ambon. The entry on Indonesian Christianity opens in 1861.
entries.sourcing: Good for how the church was built, thin for what its members said. One open-access history carries the Moluccas, Batavia and Java. It is by Indonesian and European scholars. For Ceylon the text is a Catholic sketch of 1848, and the Protestant writers it cites disagree with it. No Dutch or Malay text of the church itself was read.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is a Reformed church. Its teachers in Batavia had to agree with the Heidelberg Catechism and the Dutch Reformed Confession of Faith.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Reformed church of the Dutch East India Company. It took over the Christians the Portuguese left in the Moluccas. In Ceylon the Company's government turned its law against the Catholics, who are told in the entry on the Catholics of Dutch Ceylon.
entries.why: The Dutch East India Company was a trading firm, yet it ran a church. Its charter of 1623 asked only that it maintain the public faith. In the Moluccas village teachers carried that church, and Dutch ministers were meant to visit a few times a year.
entries.teaser: Ambon, Batavia and Ceylon, 1650 to 1815 — a trading company's church. Village teachers kept it alive, and Dutch ministers led it in the towns.
entries.longDescription:
In 1605 the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, reached Ambon and drove out the Portuguese priests. Its charter of 1623 bound it only to maintain the public faith. In two centuries it sent at least 900 ordained ministers to its lands. In the Moluccas the church ran on village teachers, called mester. The study of Aritonang and Steenbrink calls the teacher the backbone of Ambonese Christianity. He led the Sunday service and read a Malay sermon. An ordained minister was meant to visit a few times a year. The schools grew from 32 in 1633 to 54 in 1700, with 5,190 pupils. In 1673 the Ambon church ordered its teachers to come to town every two weeks, or at least every month.

Pressure also came from above. In 1677 the governor attended the mass baptism of the village of Kamarian, and the Company sent rice for the feast. In 1692 a minister complained that only the schoolchildren, the village chief and his wife came to Sunday service.

In Batavia the ministers were all Dutch, except Cornelis Senen of Banda, who was only a probationer. About 5,000 people were full members around 1700. In 1706 the church had 34 evangelists. They taught 4,873 slaves and free people. Of these, 4,440 were taught in Portuguese, 323 in Malay and 110 in Dutch. Teachers in Batavia had to agree with the Heidelberg Catechism.

Georg Werndly translated that catechism. The Malay Bible came out at Amsterdam in 1731 to 1733.

In 1753 the minister at Semarang had 1,767 Christians. Nearly half were Lutherans or Catholics. He tried not to offend them. In Ceylon the Dutch tried to make Catholic converts Reformed.
voices: João Ferreira d'Almeida — born a Catholic, minister of the Portuguese church at Batavia from 1663 to 1689, whose Portuguese New Testament was revised in 1651-52
Melchior Leijdecker — minister at Batavia from 1675 to 1701, charged in 1691 with translating the whole Bible into Malay
Georg Henric Werndly — Swiss-born minister at Makassar from 1719 to 1722, who translated the Heidelberg Catechism
The mester — the village teachers of Ambon, who led the Sunday service and read the Malay sermon
entries.legacy: By about 1650 the line between Christian and Muslim villages on Ambon was fixed. Few people crossed it after that. The whole Bible came out in Malay in 1731 to 1733. From 1815 Joseph Kam worked to renew the Company's old church in Ambon. The entry on Indonesian Christianity names him.

entries.name: Catholics of Dutch Ceylon
entries.informalName: The Church of the Night Meetings
entries.statusDescription: Tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). Its window opens in 1658, with the first Dutch law against Catholic priests. It closes in 1806, when British rule lifted the Dutch restraints. No other entry tells the church of Ceylon.
entries.sourcing: One Catholic history of 1848 carries almost all of it. The title page names no author. It was read raw; its OCR is rough in places. The Dutch Protestant side is heard only through Baldeus and Van Imhoff as the sketch quotes them, and through a modern study of the Company's church. No Portuguese, Tamil or Sinhala text was read.
entries.floorNote: No question. It is the Catholic Church, which holds the Nicene Creed.
entries.relationsSummary: This is the Catholic church that the Dutch Reformed church of the Company met in Ceylon. The Dutch banned its priests and its meetings. Priests of the Goa Oratory kept it alive from the neighboring kingdom of Kandy.
entries.why: The Dutch took Ceylon's coast and banished the Catholic priests. In 1658 they made it a crime, punishable by death, to hide one. Priests of the Goa Oratory came in disguise and kept the church going from house to house.
entries.teaser: Ceylon, 1658 to 1806 — a Catholic church under Dutch law, kept alive by priests from Goa who came in disguise and by laypeople who met at night.
entries.longDescription:
The Dutch took Ceylon's coast and banished the Catholic priests. They seized the churches and convents. At Jaffna the Dutch put several Catholics to death. The Dutch minister Baldeus says they had plotted against the government. He admits that one of them, the Jesuit Caldeiro, was not in the plot. Baldeus says he knew of it and did not report it.

A proclamation of 19 September 1658 forbade anyone to hide a Catholic priest, on pain of death. One of 11 January 1715 banned Catholic meetings. One of 8 August 1715 forbade baptism by Catholic priests. The 1848 Catholic sketch says the Dutch used force. It adds that the Protestant writers it cites deny this. Many Catholics took the new creed, partly out of fear and partly to win office. Others kept the old faith and met in their houses at night. Some fled to the inland kingdom of Kandy, whose king let them build churches. He later ordered the churches pulled down.

Late in the seventeenth century the priest Joseph Vaz of the Oratory of St Philip Neri at Goa came, disguised as a beggar. A Dutch chief persecuted him and his flock, and he had to leave the district. He went inland and spent nearly two years in prison at Kandy. Freed, he made Kandy his base. From there he visited Catholics in Dutch lands and gave them the sacraments in private, going from house to house. The bishop of Cochin named him vicar general. The Goa Oratory made him superior of the mission and sent more priests. He died at Kandy on 17 January 1711.

By 1717 the sketch counts about 70,000 converts since Vaz began. It counts over 15,000 communicants in the Jaffna district alone, and 15 large and over 400 small churches. Even then no priest dared to live in Dutch lands. They came by night in disguise. In 1743 a Kandyan king banned the faith and razed its churches. A Dutch governor, Baron Van Imhoff, wrote to his successor that the Romish priests did the Company much injury. They were, he wrote, warm in their opposition and closely united among themselves.

The Dutch gave up Ceylon to the British in 1796. Their laws stayed on the books until the regulation of 27 May 1806 took off the restraints.
voices: Joseph Vaz — priest of the Oratory of St Philip Neri at Goa, who came to Ceylon disguised as a beggar and died at Kandy on 17 January 1711
Baron Van Imhoff — Dutch governor, who wrote to his successor that the Romish priests did the Company much injury
entries.legacy: The regulation of 27 May 1806 is called a Magna Charta of the Catholics of Ceylon in the sketch of 1848. It took off the restraints that the Dutch laws had put on them. Its own words say the British government had not acted on those laws in all cases.

set.longDescription:
In 1675 a Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt, Philipp Jakob Spener, published a short book called Pia Desideria arguing that correct doctrine correctly preached was not enough. Christians needed to meet in small groups, read Scripture together, and expect their lives to change. What followed was less a new church than a renewal movement inside the Lutheran state churches, and its center became Halle, where August Hermann Francke built an orphanage that grew into a complex of schools, a printing house and a Bible institute, funded by donations and tied to correspondents across Europe, Russia, India and North America. Pietism gave German Protestantism the conversion narrative as a genre and a great body of new hymnody, and through Halle's graduates it launched one of the first organized Protestant missions sent out from Europe, when Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau sailed for the Danish trading post at Tranquebar in South India in 1706.

The Tamil church they planted went on. Fenger calls Aaron "the first native ordained" to the ministry. That was on 28 December 1733. By 1813 his list counts eleven Indian ministers.
voices: Philipp Jakob Spener — Frankfurt pastor whose Pia Desideria (1675) set the movement's program and launched its small-group meetings
August Hermann Francke — built the Halle orphanage, schools and press that became Pietism's institutional engine
Johanna Eleonora Petersen — published her own life story in 1718, one of the first autobiographies written and printed by a German woman
Johann Anastasius Freylinghausen — compiled the Halle hymnbook (1704) that carried the movement's piety in its sung form
Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg — Halle-trained, sailed in 1706 for Tranquebar in South India, translating the New Testament into Tamil
Aaron — the Indian catechist ordained on 28 December 1733, whom Fenger calls the first native ordained to the priesthood
